Preferential trade within the empire would settle this difficulty at once. Then, be goes on to point out bis views in regard to tbe way in which that might be worked out. That is a subject on which hon. gentlemen in this House, who are better acquainted with the trade relations between ourselves and the West Indies and who are
better acquainted than I am in regard to the conditions prevailing there, are better qualified to speak than I am. I give this as the opinion of a man who has studied the subject and who has arrived at that conclusion in regard to it. What I suggest in the resolution which I am moving, is that we sho'uld now "make an effort to achieve this purpose and surely I have placed sufficient evidence before the House to show that it is not such a forlorn hope that the government should remain supine and hold its hands from attempting to accomplish this end.
The third point in the resolution which I have placed before the House refers to the condition of affairs which exists between this country and Germany at the present time, and I am bound to say that I was astonished to hear the hon. Minister of Finance practically justifying Germany in granting a discrimination in favour of other countries and against Canada. I could not interpret his language in any other way and I am also astonished that neither in the speech from the Throne nor in any remarks which have fallen from the financial exponent of the government has there been any reference whatever to so important a subject as that which concerns this country in its trade relations with Germany. The situation as I understand it is that after the denunciation of the German and Belgian treaties a modus vivendi, or temporary convention, was arranged between England and Germany and that convention practically gave temporarily to each country the same advantages which had been enjoyed by each country under the former treaty, except that Canada was excluded from it. Thus it is. that, at the present time, as has been pointed out in an article on the subject in the ' National Review ' of November last, Germany having two tariffs, one a general tariff, and one a conventional tariff, grants to the United States, our keenest competitor in that market, the advantages of the lower, or conventional tariff and insists that Canadian products shall be subject to the duties imposed by the higher or general tariff. The hon. Minister of Finance and the government seem to think that this is a matter as to which we have no right to complain, and as to which it does not behoove them to say a single word. Well, Sir, they have very excellent authority as to what this act of Germany means. Let me quote to the House what was said by the Marquis of Ripon in his despatch to the Governor General of Canada on June 28, 1895 :
It must not be forgotten that, as I pointed out in my other despatches of this date, whilst the grant of preferential tariff treatment is a friend-i ly act to the country receiving it, it is an unfriendly act to countries or places excluded from it.	.
The position of affairs to-day in the empire is this : Canada gave to Great Britain

a tariff preference ; gave to Great Britain an advantage by which the goods of Great Britain came into Canada at a lower rate than the goods of countries outside the empire. Germany, disliking this action of Canada ; disliking the denunciation of the treaty, consents to a temporary renewal of the convention or treaty between England and herself but insists that Canada shall be excluded from, it. Now, I do not know whether or not this is a correct statement of the actual position of affairs to-day. I take this from an article which seems to have been written by a responsible man in the National Review of November last. I say, that if this is the condition of affairs the Canadian government were extremely remiss in not dealing with the matter either in the speech from the Throne or the budget speech, and announcing to this country whether or not tho government of Canada propose to sit calmly down and] submit to that sort of treatment from Germany ; whether or not the government of Canada have made any protest ; whether Germany is to bo allowed-on account of a preference which we granted, not to any foreign country but to Great Britain and certain of her colonies-whether Germany on account of that is to be allowed to do a friendly act to Great Britain and the rest of the colonics of the empire, and to commit an unfriendly act against Canada. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) told us that he did not know what Great Britain might do in the goodness of her heart if we granted this tariff preference. Surely the minister would not think that this isi a very ample return for anything which we may have done.
But look at the result, Mr. Speaker. In 1896 we imported from Germany $6,493,000 worth of goods ; in 1900 we imported $8,883,000 worth. In 1896 we exported to Germany $757,531 worth of goods ; in 1900 we exported to Germany $1,715,000 worth. Our trade with Germany is developing ; it would develop still further if we were not thus handicapped, for look, Sir, at the facts with respect to the trade between the United States and Germany. The trade of the United States witli Germany, so far as imports are concerned, lias increased by $3,090,000 since 1896, and so far as exports from the United States to Germany are concerned tho trade has increased by no less than $89,000,000 since 1896. Germany grants to the United States a tariff preference. Under the tariff preference the United States exports to Germany have increased $89,000,090 in the last four years. We, because we granted a tariff preference to Great Britain, are practically excluded from the benefits of that trade and the Canadian government has not one single word to say to the country when it brings down the budget, and the Minister of Finance has not one single word to say with regard to it in his financial statement. Indeed, when this

matter was dealt with by my hon. friend for Pictou (Mr. Bell), the Minister of Finance practically justified the course which Germany has pursued. I do not think that this country ought tamely to submit to treatment of that kind. I do not know of any reason why this country should riot discriminate against Germany if Germany discriminates against this country. I have endeavoured to look into the treaty conditions between England and Germany and I have not found anything still outstanding which would prevent Canada from dealing with this matter in that way. I have pointed out in the resolution a means by which we might deal with matters of that kind where we do not have fair treatment in foreign markets.
With respect to our trade relations with the United States I do not desire to say much. I entirely concur with what was said, and very wisely said, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright), that so far as our trade relations with the United States are concerned, we must use every possible effort to maintain friendly and cordial relations with that country. I know that it has been suggested by a gentleman on the other side of the House, the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), that our best course would be to raise our tariff to 50 per cent, which he says is the tariff rate of the United States. 1 am not prepared to say at the present time that I concur with that; on the other hand, I do say that our trade relations with the United States demand the attention of this government. I think we might well have had some statement from the financial exponent of the government and from so great an authority as the Minister of Trade and Commerce with respect to that. Our resolution which we have brought before the House is broad enough to cover a matter of that kind, if it is thought wise to deal with it ; but. as I have said, I do most heartily concur with the view that so far as the great country to the south of us is concerned, we should do nothing which should be misunderstood by that republic and which might provoke a breach of the very cordial relations which at present exists between the two countries.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am very sorry indeed to have detained the House at such great length, but I was obliged to do so because I had a great many extracts-more than I liked-to read to the House. Just one word in conclusion. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce has taunted us with the suggestion that we are likely to remain in opposition, as he says, for the next 25 years. Well, I do not know that the hon. gentleman (Sir Richard Cartwright) is in a much better position to form an opinion in regard to that than the rest of us. But I would like to say this : I am sorry that the minister (Sir Richard Cart-
wright) did not see fit to put any higher ideal before members of this House and before any political party iu this country, than the obtaining or retaining of power. I understood the hon. gentleman to suggest that such is the greatest possible good to any political party at any possible cost. There are, Mr. Speaker, things of more importance to any political party in this country than to obtain power or even to retain power. I think, Sir, that an honourable adherence to honourable principles professed in opposition or in power is a thing more to be regarded than even the obtaining of power itself. I think the upholding of the standard of public opinion in this country, the upholding of the standard of public life in this country, is of more importance to any political party than the obtaining or retaining of power. I think that to stand for the unity of the people of this country and to suppress any cry of race or creed that may be raised, is a matter of greater importance to any political party in Canada than is the effort to obtain or retain power. For my part, speaking for the party I have the honour to lead in this House, I say that we shall endeavour to carry out the principles which we have professed in this resolution and the principles which we have at all times professed in the past; of endeavouring to uphold the industries of Canada, to develop the resources of this country, to maintain the integrity and unity of the empire. In doing this, Sir, I think we shall be discharging our duty, and if we discharge our duty. I am sure that we need not fear the issue. Mr. Speaker. I beg to move the resolution of which I have already given notice, as follows .-
That all the words after ' that ' in the proposed motion be left out, and the following sub-stitued therefor :
That, in the opinion of this House, the welfare of this country requires a pronounced policy of adequate protection and encouragement at all times to the labour, agricultural, manufacturing, mining and other industrial interests of Canada ;
That, in the opinion of this House, the adoption a policy of mutual trade preference within the empire would prove of great benefit to the mother country and to the colonies, and would greatly promote the prosperity, unity and progress of the empire as a whole, and that the present time, when the Commonwealth of Australia is laying the foundation of its fiscal system, is particularly opportune for taking prompt and energic steps towards the furtherance of this object.
This House is further of opinion that equivalent or adequate duti'es should be imposed by Canada upon the products and manufactures of countries not within the empire in all cases where such countries fail to admit Canadian products and manufactures upon fair terms, and that the government should take for this purpose all such available measures as may be found necessary.

Mr. Speaker, from the first day of this session there have been rumours whispered from ear to ear through the corridors of this House and sometimes heard also in the streets of this city, that the new opposition of His Majesty, when once constituted and organized, would spring upon us a surprise in the shape of a new fiscal policy. As time went on statements were made in the press that this new policy would surprise the government and stagger the Liberal party as soon as it was announced. We have it now, fresh and brand new, from the lips of my hon. friend, and lo and behold, it is the same old national policy.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: Hear, hear.

The same old national policy, with a few adornments which, instead of taking from its native deformity, only add to it- It is the same old national policy which we have fought in past elections, and which, after an experience of some twenty years, has been twice rejected by tbe people at the polls. There was nothing new under tbe sun some three or four thousand years ago ; there is nothing new in the Conservative party to-day. I take the motion of my hon. friend, as you have just had it from his hands, and it reads as follows :-
That, in tbe opinion of this House, tbe welfare of this country requires a pronounced policy of adequate protection and encouragement at all times to the labour, agricultural, manufacturing, mining and other industrial interests-of Canada.
I take up the famous resolution which was moved in this House twfgity-two years ago, and it reads as follows
This House is of the opinion that the welfare of Canada requires the adoption of a national policy, which, by a judicious readjustment of the tariff, will benefit and foster the agricultural, the mining, the manufacturing and other interests of the Dominion; that such a policy will retain in Canada thousands of our fellow-countrymen now obliged to expatriate themselves in search of the employment denied them at home.
This is the policy repeated in the resolution of my hon. friend the new leader of the opposition ; and my hon. friend tells us, and apparently seriously, that the policy which he now reaffirms, has had a great success. But he forgets that though it was designed to keep our own people at home, yet one result of that policy was that his own province lost one representative in this House. The hon. gentleman also tells us that he wants tp go back to the principles of the national policy and have them reenacted. Let us cast a glance at what that policy lias done. At the time the national policy was adopted in 1880. tbe trade of the country amounted to 8203,000,000 ; in

1896, when it was put an end to, the trade of the country had increased to $239,000,000, an increase of $36,000,000 in sixteen years. In 1896-7, we adopted a new tariff -a revenue tariff, as I shall explain in a few minutes-and in the course of four years the trade of the country increased to $381,000,000, an increase of $142,000,000 in the four years. On this comparison of the results of the policy adopted by this government and the results of the policy proposed by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, I leave the people and the House to judge of the merits of the two policies.
It is refreshing, however, to hear the statement made by my hon. friend, in view of the attitude which has been maintained by his party ever since this debate has commenced. We have had the statement made by these gentlemen day in and day out that the present tariff is still a protective tariff, that there is nothing changed, that we have the same policy that we had up to 1896. If the tariff which we have at the present moment is the same protective tariff which we had formerly, what is the use, I want to know, of taking up the time of the House to argue that we should have a protective tariff ? Why should we have this new proposition solemnly made by my hon. friend, 1 that in the opinion of this House the welfare of this country requires a pronounced policy of adequate protection,' when these hon. gentlemen tell us that we have adequate protection to-day ?
But, Sir, I care not by what name the policy of the present government is characterized. I care not whether it pleases my hon. friends on the other side to call it protection or free trade or a revenue tariff. There is only on^ difference between us and gentlemen on the other side of the House. We agree with them that the revenue of the country ought to be levied by means of customs duties ; but there is this difference between us, that while they would levy those duties only for the benefit of individuals, we levy them for the benefit of the revenue first and foremost.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have been dilating on the idea that the present tariff is a protective tariff. So far as protection is an incident of the tariff, there is no doubt that it is. There is a great deal of protection yet in the tariff, and there must be a great deal of protection in any tariff of customs duties. If we impose a duty of 25 per cent on an article of any kind whatever, it is manifest that the manufacturer of similar goods in this country must have the benefit of 25 per cent in favour of his goods. So far there is ft great deal of protection in the tariff ; if I were to express my own mind, perhaps I would say there is more in it than I would desire. But we have to reckon according to the condition of things that exists to-day. We have to maintain a tariff of customs duties;

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: but, again I repeat, the difference that exists between us and gentlemen on the other side is this. Our first consideration, in imposing duties, is to produce revenue and if, as an incident, the manufacturers derive advantage, they are welcome to it. But gentlemen on the other side imposed duties not with the view of levying a revenue and putting money into the treasury, but of putting money in the pockets of private individuals. There is the difference between the two policies. Which of these policies is to prevail in this country ? Is it the policy of protection pure and simple of hon. gentlemen opposite ?
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says hear, hear. I am quite content to abide by the result. Is it to be the policy of protection pure and simple or that adopted in 1897, not based on protection, but in which protection is an incident ? The result of the policy adopted in 1897, is that the country has never been so prosperous.
But that is not free trade as they have it in England.

If these hon. gentlemen when they quote my words, would do me the simple justice of quoting them in their entirety, and not clip out a part of any utterance of mine, they would find that at no time have the Liberal party ever pretended that, if they came into power, they would adopt immediately free trade as it is in England. But what we have said again and again is that while we believe in free trade as a theory, we know that we are bound to raise a revenue by a customs tariff, and it will take many years before we could have free trade as it is in England. But apart from this, there is this consideration to be borne in mind. There has never been a period of time in the history of Canada when our manufacturing industries were so safe and secure as they are at present. If you had a tariff based, as in the years from 1879 to 1896, upon a protection basis, you would have the duties continually changed from one year to another, as was the case in those days. You would have, as we had under the late government, an incessant procession of tariff tinkerers from the different cities of Canada to the office of the Finance Minister. There never was a year from 1879 to 1896-or at least there never was a period of three years-when there was not some tinkering of the tariff. One man would find that some invention in the United States or Great Britain had lowered the prices of the products he was making, and instead of exercising his enterprise and ingenuity to overcome the difficulty, instead of putting more money into his business, he came to the Finance Minister and obtained some modification of the tariff. Then what happened ? It was then found that the man

wlio was benefited by tbe change in the tariff was producing an article which was the raw material of some other industry. These other manufacturers came to the Minister of Finance again, and again there was more tinkering. But when the public at large understand that they have nothing to fear, when they know that the basis of the tariff is not to please this one or that one but to raise a revenue, they are aware that so long as the financial conditions remain as they are, there is to be no change in the tariff whatever, and instead of looking forward with dread to the deliverance of the budget speech, as used to be the case in former years, they know there will be no change and no reason to fear. They know that there will be no change in the tariff except when a general revision of it becomes necessary. This is the policy which we propose to maintain and upon which we take issue with hon. gentlemen opposite.
Now, I come to the other part of my hon. friend's resolution which is in these terms :
That, In the opinion of this House, the adoption of a policy of mutual trade preference within the empire would prove of great benefit to the mother country and to the colonies and would greatly promote the prosperity, unity and progress of the empire as a whole.
With regard to this policy, I am ready and willing, and even anxious to engage the issue with my hon. friends opposite. Let us understand, first of all, where we are. They want a mutual preference with England. Well, before we lay that policy before the Canadian people, let us understand well what is the object of the Conservative party. My hon. friend has said that they are protectionists, that they stand upon the old policy of protection. Protection against whom ? Against the United States ? Yes. Against Germany ? Yes. Against France ? Yes. Against England? Yes. Their policy is a policy of protection against England as well as every other country. This fact has been made plain to-day by my hon. friend. Before I go further X want it to be well understood on both sides that the main object which the Conservative party has in view to-day and which they will carry out, should they attain office again, is to maintain the policy of protection against Great Britain as well as every other nation in the world.
Hear, hear.

This was laid down only a few days ago by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell). My hon. friend delivered himself as follows on this point :
That question was settled in 1879.
He was speaking of the question of protection in favour of Canadian industries :
One of the objections made at that time to the establishment of a protective tariff in Canada was that it was an unfriendly act towards
Great Britain, a country which depended upon its manufactures, which prized its foreign trade. It was argued then that possibly the British government might even disallow our protective tariff on the ground that it was striking at British trade. But the men of that day who passed the national policy, who put the national policy into operation, had considered all these things, they met the objection that it was an unfriendly act to Great Britain, they faced that bugbear, for bugbear it was, they were not frightened by it, and they faced that consideration in 1879, and settled it then. Their protective tariff was not hampered or impaired, or emasculated, by sentimental consideration for the manufacturers of Great Britain. Nothing of the kind was allowed to affect the efficiency of the national policy at that time, and nothing of the kind should be allowed to affect the efficiency of the national policy to-dqy. Therefore, I say if this administration is ever brought to their knees, when pressure of hard times will come to the manufacturing industries of this country, and bring them to that point where they will approach the government for relief, if this government is then going to maintain the position of a protectionist administration, it will have to look carefully into the effect of this preferential tariff.
If the hon. gentleman meant anything, he meant this, that so strong is the view of the party to which he belonged in favour of protection, that in its favour even the preferential tariff had to give way. There is no ambiguity in this policy. We know where we are. The policy of these hon. gentlemen is to maintain protection against Great Britain.
Before I go further let me say this, and I do not say it by way of rebuke or reproach, that if these hon. gentlemen believe that protection is the best policy for Canada, they are quite right in applying it against Great Britain. For my own part, although I am devotedly attached to Great Britain, if a conflict of interests were ever to take place between us, I would stand by my native land. Therefore if hon. gentlemen on the other side believe that protection should be maintained against Great Britain, I have no fault to find with them. But in the name of common sense I ask them if they believe in a policy of protection against Great Britain, what can they say if the people of Great Britain believe that a policy of free trade with all the world is the best protection they can have ?
Why, Sir, there must be the same rule on one side as on the other. If it is to be protection of Canada against Great Britain, it must be protection of Great Britain against Canada. Or, if the same rule should apply on either side, how are you going to speak of mutuality of preference where you have protection in Canada and free trade in Great Britain ? These gentlemen will go to Great Britain in order to proffer their policy of protection for Canada and a preference for Canada in the British markets. Why, they will be told by the people of Great Britain : You may believe in protection, but we believe in free trade, and
1C23

if you will not give us a preference we will not give you a preference ; and if you maintain a policy of protection against us, we shall maintain a policy of free trade, which is most in our own interest. I know that these hon. gentlemen hope, and even believe, that the people of Great Britain are turning their hacks upon the policy of free trade. They see the day coming, as they think, when Great Britain will become protectionist, as it was at one time. But if that is their hope, in what position will the Canadian producer be if the views of the Canadian Conservatives are to prevail in England ? Canada will be a protectionist, and so will Great Britain-and what mutual preference could you have under such circumstances ? Let us consider this case as we should then find it. I suppose that my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will obtain power some day. I will not discuss the exact time when that will come about. He found fault with my suggestion of a period of twenty-five years in opposition for him. Well, if he objects to that, let us say that he obtains power in fifty years. After that, he goes to Great Britain to present the view he has advocated here-for he cannot attain the object of his policy unless there is mutual and concurrent action by Great Britain and Canada. He goes to Sheffield, or Manchester, or Birmingham, or some other of the great business and manufacturing centres of Great Britain. He speaks before a meeting of working men, and says : We have a trade policy to propose to you ; the agriculture of Great Britain is inadequate ; it cannot feed you, and you have to import your food from all parts of the world. Canada cannot to-day, but by-and-by will be able to supply the whole of your food requirements : Give us a preference in your markets ; put a duty on corn, butter, cheese and everything that you eat that comes from abroad and that we can grow, but exempt from that duty all the products of Canada. The workingman would probably say : For the sake of the bond that exists between us I might put a tax on our food and exempt the products coming from your country ; but you know that I am a maker of manufactured products and I want a market for my goods ; I want a market in Canada ; and, since you want us to exempt your products from taxes, no doubt you will exempt our products from duty when we send them to your markets. But my hon. friend will say : No, X do not propose that ; I am a protectionist, and believe in protection for our Canadian manufactures ; therefore, I do not propose to exempt your products from a tax which affects products of all kinds ; but, while I do not propose to exempt your products from taxation, I want you to exempt our products from the tax which I wish you to put upon the products of other countries. Do you not think that the workingman will say : This is a rather cool proposal ; you want

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: me to tax my food for your benefit, but you are not prepared to exempt my products from taxation for my benefit; you want me to allow you to smite me on the right cheek and then have me turn the other cheek to be smitten also. Such a policy would not be received in Great Britain- it is not to be taken seriously.
Oh, oh.
It is not a thing to be discussed seriously.
Oh, oh.
Hear, hear.

But it is somewhat difficult to convince hon. gentlemen, it is difficult to convince men who do not want to be convinced ; it is difficult to be heard when men will not hear you. It is difficult to convince men when they do not

want to see. Hon. gentlemen opposite are like the pagan idols, they liave eyes but they do not see, ears but they do not hear. Here is the language of Mr. Chamberlain upon this point, which has been quoted again and again, delivered before this very Congress of the Chambers of Commerce in the year 1896 :
But up to the present time we have not been agreed as to the methods by which this object may be reached. It appears to me that there are only three lines of progress which have been suggested to accomplish this great object. The first of them is a proposal that the colonies should abandon their own fiscal system and should adopt ours, that they should carry out fully the doctrines of free trade, that they should open their markets not only to us but to all the world, and that they should abandon entirely the protective duties upon which now they rest very largely for the revenues which they collect. That is a proposal which is supported by the Cohden Club, by the extreme, or perhaps I may say by orthodox free-traders, and there is no doubt a good deal to be said for it. I do not deny that possibly it might be to all concerned the best solution ; at the same time I am hound to point out that that would not bring about commercial union in the sense in which we have generally understood the word, because that would be in the direction of cosmopolitan union, but it would offer no particular advantage to the trade of the empire as such. But what is to my mind a much more fatal objection is the fact that, speaking generally, the colonies will not adopt this proposal.
I think be was speaking truly there.
We must consider it, therefore, as a council of protection, and if we are to wait until the colonies generally are converted to our views in regard to the advantages of free trade, let us recognize the fact that we must postpone the hope of commercial union to the Greek Kalends. General free trade in this country has been developed, no doubt, to the great advantage of this country for the period of half a century, but in spite of that it has made no converts. We do not find-again I am speaking generally because I know there are exceptions-that there is any considerable approach to our system on the part of the colonies, and there is no approach at all to it on the part of foreign countries. Well, I pass on to the second proposal which has been laid before a similar congress to this, which found expression at the great congress at Ottawa a year or two ago,-that is a proposal which has been favoured by some of our principal colonies and described with great force and elegance by leading colonists, and it is the very reverse, in spirit at any rate, of the proposal which I have just been considering ; for whereas the first proposal requires that the colonies should abandon their system in favour nf ours, this proposal requires that we should abandon our system in favour of theirs.
That is bringing the proposition to its true basis.
It is, in effect, that while the colonies should be left absolutely free to impose what protective duties they please both upon foreign countries and upon British commerce, they should be required to make a small discrimination in favour of British trade, in return for which we are expected to change our whole system and to impose duties on food and on raw material. Well, Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
I express again my own opinion when I say that there is not the slightest chance that in any reasonable time this country, or the parliament of this country, would adopt so one-sided an agreement. The foreign trade of this country is so large, and the foreign trade of the colonies is comparatively so small that a small preference given to us upon that foreign trade by the colonies would make so slight a difference, would be so slight a benefit to the total volume of our trade, that I do not believe the working classes of this country would consent to make a revolutionary change for what they would think to be an infinitesimal game. Well, you will see that so far we have only arrived at a deadlock. We have a proposal by British free-traders which is rejected by the colonies, we have a proposal by colonial protectionists which is rejected by Great Britain.
That is the true position.
We have, therefore, if we are to make any progress at all, to seek a third course in which there should be give and take on both sides-
Hear, hear.

Hon. gentlemen had better wait a little before they cheer.
-in which neither side will pedantically adhere to preconceived conclusions, in which the good of the whole shall subordinate the separate interests of parts. And I admit that, if I understand it correctly, I find the germs of such a proposal in a resolution which is to be submitted to you on behalf of the Toronto Board of Trade. What is that resolution? I hope I correctly explain it. That resolution I understand to be one for the creation of a British Zollverein or customs union which would establish at once practically free trade throughout the British Empire, but would leave the contracting parties free to make their own arrangements with regard to duties upon foreign goods; except that this is an essential condition of the proposal that Great Britain shall consent to replace moderate duties upon certain articles which are of large production in the colonies. Now, if I have rightly understood it, these articles would comprise corn, meat, wool and sugar, and perhaps othe_r articles of enormous consumption in this country which are at present largely produced in the colonies, and which might he, under such an arrangement, wholly produced in the colonies, and wholly produced by British labour. On the other hand, as I have said, the colonies, while maintaining their duties upon foreign imports, would agree to a free interchange of commodities with the rest of the empire, and would cease to place protective duties upon any product of British labour. That is the principal of the German Zollverein; that is the principle which underlies the federation of the United States of .America; and I do not doubt for a moment that if it were adopted it would be the strongest bond of union between the British race throughout the world. (Cheers.) I say that such a proposal as that might commend itself even to an orthodox free trader. It would he the greatest advance that free trade has ever made since it was first advocated by Mr. Cohden, to extend its doctrines permanently to more than 300 millions of the human race, and to communities many of which are amongst the most thriving, the most prosperous and the most rapidly increasing in the world. On the other hand, it would open up to the colonies an almost
unlimited market for their agricultural and other productions.
Row,.that is the condition upon which the man who has been relied upon to favour the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, says that you can negotiate free trade within the empire. If hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House are ready to go to England and negotiate upon that basis, they may do so. They can agitate public opinion upon that basis, but so long as they go to England as protectionists it is the essence of absurdity-I can use no other word-for them to expect a hearing. That is not the only occasion upon which Mr. Chamberlain has spoken upon this subject. He spoke a few months ago at the last congress of the Chambers of Commerce which took place in June, 1900. In parliament, in 1900, on the floor of the House of Commons he spoke again on this subject. Speaking on the motion of the hon. member for Elland, he said :
The hon. member for Elland referred to a proposal which has been made by the London Chamber of Commerce for a, fiscal arrangement with the colonies, which is, indeed, a proposal for an Imperial Zollverein. I have never done anything of the sort. It is one of those mistakes of which I am so largely the victim, and which perhaps it would hardly be worth while to contradict until the occasion becomes urgent. All I have done is to point out that, following the language used by Lord Ripon, my predecessor, if there is to be any kind of fiscal arrangement with the colonies, the only form which I myself think would be viewed with the slightest favour in this country would be an Imperial Zollverein, in which there should be free trade between the whole empire, and duties of some kind as against other countries. But I have not proposed that; I have only stated that that alone seems to be a proposal which might be seriously considered.
Allusion has been made very otten to my trip to England and to the position I took there. The position I took there was this: I acted like a reasonable man, I saw at once that it could not be possible, so great is the free trade sentiment in England, to have a mutuality of preference so long as we continue to levy customs duties upon English goods. But, the moment we are ready-it may take a long time, but I hope that some day it shall come-to discard our tariff, the moment we come to the doctrine of free trade, then it is possible to have a commercial mutual preference based upon free trade in the empire. There is free trade to-day between seventy-five million people in the United States, there is free trade between forty million Germans, there is free trade between thirty-six million Frenchmen, and if it is possible to have free trade between 300,000,000 of British subjects you would have the greatest commercial policy the world has ever seen. But, how can hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House hope to have any hearing whatever so long as they
go to England and say :	We will protect
ourselves against your goods and at the same time we want you to give us free trade for our goods '? The thing is absurd. That is the policy that hon. gentlemen are proposing.
I come to the third proposal of my hon. friend in his resolution. I may say that I am glad to hear the declaration made by the hon. gentleman on this subject, and I think it is a considerable back down from the terms he has proposed in his resolution. In his resolution the hon. gentleman says :
This House is further of opinion that equivalent or adequate duties should be imposed by Canada upon the products and manufactures of countries not within the empire in all cases where such countries fail to admit Canadian products and manufactures upon fair terms, and that the government should take for this purpose all such available measures as may be found necessary.
When I read this resolution before it was commented upon by the hon. gentleman, I assumed that it applied to the United States which maintains a high tariff against us, and I would not be prepared to adopt it upon this ground. I am glad that the hon. gentleman has taken a more sensible view and that he takes the position that however unfair we may think the United States tariff is against us, it is not practically enforced against us, because it is directed against and it applies to the whole world. However unfair we think it, my hon. friend thinks it would not be right for us to follow in the same direction and elevate our tariff as high as the United States tariff is.

Will the right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) allow me to interrupt him ? I said that I was not prepared at present to coincide altogether with the views of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), but that I thought that the trade relations between this country and the United States was a subject that might fairly claim the attention of the government.

I might fairly claim the attention of the government. Well, 1 thought it claimed the attention of the opposition also, but I am wrong in believing that. My hon. friend says :	I wash my
hands of the whole thing, the government may consider it, but as to this I do not advise. I have no objection to advise as far as Germany is concerned, but as far as the United States are concerned I do not advise. Well, if the hon. gentleman will not advise, I will. I have no hesitation in facing the situation. And when lion, gentlemen opposite, because we must assume that my hon. friend is voicing the sentiments of his friends upon this subject, tell us that we should elevate our tariff to the height of the American tariff, I take issue with them altogether. The tariff of the people of Canada is to be determined by the people them-

selves not from any consideration of the tariffs of the United States or of other countries, but simply of the consideration of what best suits the Canadian people. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House cannot maintain their doctrine; they would be blocked at the first step that they would take if they were to try to elevate our tariff to the height of the American tariff. I will take one or two articles. The American duty on wool is 11 cents per pound. Our duty Is practically nil; wool is practically free. Would hon. gentlemen opposite advise us to elevate our tariff to the height of the American tariff on wool ? Would they propose to raise the duty on wool to 11 cents a pound because that happens to be the duty imposed under the American tariff ? The thing is absurd. Hon. gentlemen know that it cannot be done and they simply placed before the people a proposition there which the hon. leader of the opposition recants but which may go abroad here and there because it may affect this or that interest. Let us face the situation bravely like men, let us resolve that whatever may be the American tariff we shall be guided only by the measure of what is in our own interest in this respect. In regard to the German tariff, I have a word to say to my hon. friend. I find no fault with the manner in which he has approached this question. This is a question of some importance and which deserves to be very seriously considered. Some years ago we found that the treaty of Great Britain with Germany was a great block in our path. It affected our commercial liberties. We could not give a preference to Great Britain because we would have to give it to Germany.
For years and years the Conservative party when they were in office tried to get these treaties abolished, but they could not succeed. When the Liberal party came into power they were at once successful in that direction. It is refreshing to hear the explanation given us the other day by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) as to the manner in which we accomplished that which his political friends failed In accomplishing for many years. He told us that by our preferential tariff we blundered into such a position that it forced the hand of the mother country. Well, I would not quarrel with the hon. gentleman as it is past six o'clock, but whether we blundered into it or not, yet if we did blunder into it, I call his attention to the fact that even when we do blunder we can accomplish things that he and his friends in power could not accomplish even by design ?
Hear, hear.

And so, if we blundered and if they designed, they failed in their design and we carried our point. Sir, if we forced the hand of England to denounce the German treaty it is not be-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
cause we had any hostility against Germany ; it is not because we did not want to trade with Germany, but simply because we wanted our freedom of action restored to us. In this we succeeded. My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) told us truthfully that there were two tariffs in Germany ; the general tariff and the conventional tariff ; the general tariff being the higher and the conventional tariff the lower. Great Britain negotiated a new treaty and obtained the advantage of the conventional tariff. The United States to-day have the advantage of the conventional tariff, and I am not without hope that we also shall have some day the advantage of the conventional tariff. But before we bring this question to the angry discussion of parliament and of the country, my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will agree with me that we should exhaust every confidential mode of obtaining this object. And when we have adopted every confidential mode that we can adopt, then if we fail we shall have to come before the House and frankly say that we have failed, and we may have to adopt some other method. But until that time arrives my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will, I think, agree with me that it is better to leave this matter to be dealt with confidentially between the Imperial government and the Canadian authorities.
There is one thing as to which 1 am glad to agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax). In his peroration he uttered some very noble sentiments which I trust shall find echo in North Bruce the day after to-morrow. The hon. gentleman told us that he was adverse to having anything like racial questions introduced. I do not know if his attention has been drawn to the paragraph in the paper which is his organ, if he has an organ in North Bruce, and which referring to the contest now going on in that constituency spoke of the ' Tarte-Laurier combination.' This 1 Tarte-Laurier combination' referred to in that style in a Conservative paper published in a riding where a contest is now pending has a meaning which we all understand very well. It has a meaning the very reverse of the language spoken a moment ago by my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) when he stated that he did not want any racial cry raised in this country. I trust that his words therefore will go to North Bruce to be pitted against the language of the newspaper which supports his candidate in that election.
